Bhaṅga, ‘hemp,’ is mentioned in the Atharvaveda.^1 In the
Rigveda^2 it is an epithet of Soma, presumably^3 in the sense of
‘intoxicating,’ which then came to designate hemp.^4
1) xi. 6, 15; conceivably in Śāṅkh-
āyana Āraṇyaka, xii. 14, but not prob-
ably.
2) ix. 61, 13.
3) Schrader, Prehistoric Antiquities, 299.
4) Hence the modern ‘Bang’ or
Bhang,’ an intoxicant made from the
dried leaves and small stalks of hemp,
taken either by smoking or by eating
when mixed up into a sweetmeat.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 68;
Grierson, Indian Antiquary, 23, 260;
Yule and Burnell, Hobson-Jobson, s.v.
Bang.

Bhaṅgāśvina is the name of the father of Ṛtuparna in the
Baudhāyana Śrauta Sūtra.^1 In the Mahābhārata^2 he is called
Bhāṅgāsuri. In the Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra^3 mention is
made of Ṛtuparṇa-Kayovadhī as the Bhaṅgyaśvinau.
1) xx. 12.
2) iii. 2745.
3) xxi. 20; Caland, Zeitschrift der
Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft,
57, 745.

Bhaṅgya-śravas is the name of a man in the Taittirīya
Āraṇyaka.^1
1) Weber, Indische Studien, 1, 78.
